title: UniHam: A Large-Scale SOC-Complete Dataset and Benchmark for Hamiltonian Learning in Materials
authors: Yuewen Huang, Pin Chen, Yutong Lu
abstract: Accurate prediction of electronic Hamiltonians would enable broad property inference while avoiding the high computational cost of Density Functional Theory (DFT). However, progress toward general-purpose materials foundation models is limited by a data bottleneck: existing Hamiltonian datasets are typically small, lack structural diversity, and often omit essential relativistic physics such as spin--orbit coupling (SOC). We therefore construct UniHam, a large-scale Hamiltonian dataset and benchmark suite comprising 100,000+ DFT-computed complex-valued Hermitian Hamiltonians with full SOC, covering 72 elements and a wide range of crystal geometries and symmetries (spanning diverse lattice types and space-group families). Building on UniHam, we benchmark two representative state-of-the-art models under a standardized protocol and introduce complementary evaluation metrics that jointly assess three dimensions: (i) Hamiltonian reconstruction accuracy, (ii) out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization across composition/symmetry shifts, and (iii) the ability to support downstream property prediction from the predicted Hamiltonians. Experiments on UniHam demonstrate that the proposed benchmark and metrics effectively differentiate model capabilities, revealing intrinsic SOC- and element-dependent failure modes, large variations in compositional OOD robustness, and the necessity of spectral-level evaluation to assess whether Hamiltonian predictions reliably support downstream electronic-structure properties. Overall, UniHam provides a reproducible, SOC-complete benchmark that can sharpen model comparisons and accelerate the development of next-generation foundation models for quantum materials.

infographic.key_insight: UniHam benchmarks Hamiltonian learning with spin–orbit coupling (SOC), showing that reconstruction accuracy alone cannot establish reliability for downstream electronic-property prediction.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Learning reliable electronic Hamiltonians could reduce reliance on costly DFT calculations while supporting property inference across diverse materials.
method: Construct 100,000+ DFT-computed complex-valued Hermitian Hamiltonians with full SOC across 72 elements.
Benchmark two representative state-of-the-art models under a standardized protocol.
Evaluate reconstruction accuracy, composition/symmetry OOD generalization, and downstream property prediction.
infographic.evidence_signal: The benchmark reveals SOC- and element-dependent failure modes, substantial variation in compositional OOD robustness, and the need for spectral-level evaluation.
infographic.watch_item: Coverage of 72 elements does not guarantee reliability on unseen compositions or symmetries; validate spectral and downstream-property accuracy before deployment.
infographic.paper_title: UniHam: A Large-Scale SOC-Complete Dataset and Benchmark for Hamiltonian Learning in Materials

title: Strain-dependent Dynamics of Interactions of Iodine-vacancy pairs in CsPbI3: A DFT and Machine-Learning Molecular Dynamics Study
authors: Donggeun Kang, Seongju Lee, Yonggoon Jeon
abstract: Iodine-vacancy migration and association are important factors in the structural stability of halide perovskites. Although neighboring vacancies have been suggested to form energetically favorable pairs, their stability and reconfiguration under finite-temperature lattice deformation remain unclear. Here, we combine machine-learning molecular dynamics (MLMD) and density functional theory (DFT) to investigate neighboring iodine vacancies in tilted CsPbI3 under isotropic and biaxial strain. The MLMD trajectories reveal a nonmonotonic dependence of short-time hopping fractions on strain, with strong isotropic compression favoring point-like separation and tension promoting pair-preserving relay hopping. Notably, biaxial compression produces distinct orientation-dependent responses: vacancy pairs initially aligned with the compressed plane preferentially undergo separation, whereas those perpendicular to the plane predominantly exhibit relay hopping. Complementary static calculations using DFT and the SevenNet-0 potential yield repulsive interactions for all configurations examined. These findings highlight the importance of finite-temperature dynamics and strain-dependent local geometry in understanding vacancy-pair stability and reconfiguration in halide perovskites.

infographic.key_insight: Strain controls iodine-vacancy pair dynamics in CsPbI3: strong isotropic compression favors separation, tension promotes pair-preserving relay hopping, and biaxial compression produces orientation-dependent responses.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Strain engineering may help control defect migration and reconfiguration relevant to the structural stability of halide perovskites.
method: Machine-learning molecular dynamics of neighboring iodine vacancies in tilted CsPbI3 under isotropic and biaxial strain.
Analysis of short-time hopping fractions, pair separation, and relay hopping.
Static vacancy-interaction calculations using DFT and the SevenNet-0 potential.
infographic.evidence_signal: MLMD shows nonmonotonic strain-dependent hopping and orientation-dependent behavior under biaxial compression, while DFT and SevenNet-0 yield repulsive interactions for every examined configuration.
infographic.watch_item: Short-time hopping behavior does not establish long-term vacancy-pair stability or device-scale degradation.
infographic.paper_title: Strain-dependent Dynamics of Interactions of Iodine-vacancy pairs in CsPbI3: A DFT and Machine-Learning Molecular Dynamics Study

title: Benchmarking language models and agents for scientific reasoning in evolving materials laboratories
authors: Xuyu Dong, Yixuan Li, Jianguo Huang, Feng Chen, Yiyun Zhou, Bo An
abstract: Large language models and the multi-agent systems built around them could accelerate materials discovery by connecting scientific knowledge with experimental decisions. Existing benchmarks establish capabilities in domain knowledge, multimodal interpretation and scientific tool use. As language models increasingly support materials research workflows, their ability to distinguish closely related material states and reason accurately with quantitative evidence remains insufficiently evaluated. These abilities are essential for comparing material responses, assessing mechanisms and maintaining reliable judgements as experimental evidence accumulates. We introduce MatScope to evaluate three connected capabilities. M1 tests unaided, condition-specific reasoning through 200 tasks spanning ten research functions, using aluminium and high-entropy alloys as representative material systems. M2 tests agent-assisted transfer of related knowledge to unresolved materials questions. MatEvoBench-20 tests initial forecasts across scientific dependency chains and revisions of still-hidden responses as observations accumulate. Across eleven model deployments, including GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1, given-input calculations and many physical explanations are handled well. Fine-grained response estimates, comparisons between similar states and quantitatively supported choices remain substantially weaker. Related literature improves selected estimates, while condition and baseline mismatches limit transfer. Progressive observations calibrate some downstream responses and destabilize earlier accurate predictions. MatScope establishes measurable targets for developing reliable scientific reasoning in future self-evolving materials laboratories and materials-aware world models.

infographic.key_insight: Models handle many calculations and physical explanations well but struggle to distinguish similar material states and make quantitatively supported decisions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Reliable AI-assisted materials discovery requires condition-specific reasoning and evidence updates that improve predictions without destabilizing accurate ones.
method: M1: Test unaided, condition-specific reasoning across ten research functions.
M2: Evaluate agent-assisted transfer of related knowledge to unresolved materials questions.
MatEvoBench-20: Assess initial forecasts and revisions as experimental observations accumulate.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across eleven model deployments, M1's 200 aluminium and high-entropy alloy tasks and complementary evaluations reveal weaker fine-grained estimates, state comparisons and quantitative choices.
infographic.watch_item: Literature transfer can fail when conditions or baselines differ, and new observations can destabilize previously accurate predictions.
infographic.paper_title: Benchmarking language models and agents for scientific reasoning in evolving materials laboratories

title: MOTIF: LLM-Defined Material Taxonomies for OOD Property Prediction via Invariant Feature Selection
authors: Gwangseon Jang, Sieun Yun, Dong Ho Lee, Kyong-Ha Lee, Chanuk Lim, Jin Woo Choi
abstract: Out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization remains a central challenge in materials property prediction, where models must extrapolate to novel chemistries beyond the training distribution. While large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong scientific reasoning, their direct use for quantitative prediction remains limited. To address this, we systematically evaluate multiple roles for LLM assistance, finding that only taxonomy-based grouping consistently improves OOD generalization over a strong kNN+GBT baseline. Building on this, we here propose MOTIF, a framework that leverages LLMs not as predictors, but as generators of candidate taxonomies that partition materials into chemically meaningful environments. These taxonomies are evaluated via training-only pseudo-OOD validation, and only those that improve generalization are retained. Invariant feature selection is then applied within each accepted taxonomy, followed by gated aggregation across taxonomies. We evaluate on 2D halide perovskites, where bandgap prediction must generalize across distinct organic spacer families. On this benchmark, MOTIF reduces mean OOD MAE from 0.122 to 0.111 eV. Under a frozen dev/test protocol, the deployable configuration further improves errors from 0.123 to 0.117 eV (electronic bandgap) and from 0.181 to 0.173 eV (optical bandgap). Beyond this primary task, we validate transferability across additional materials datasets, including 3D perovskite solar cell efficiencies and Matbench benchmarks with structure-based splits. Across domains, MOTIF consistently improves robustness under distribution shift, outperforming expert-defined groupings, rule-based heuristics, and clustering baselines, while remaining competitive with strong classical selection methods. These results demonstrate that LLMs are most effective not as predictors, but as tools for discovering structure in data.

infographic.key_insight: MOTIF improves out-of-distribution materials property prediction by using LLMs to propose chemical taxonomies rather than predict numerical properties directly.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework can improve prediction robustness for unfamiliar material families by selecting features that generalize across chemically meaningful groups.
method: Use LLMs to generate candidate taxonomies that partition materials into chemical environments.
Retain taxonomies that improve training-only pseudo-OOD validation, then apply invariant feature selection within each.
Combine predictions across accepted taxonomies using gated aggregation.
infographic.evidence_signal: On 2D halide perovskites, mean OOD bandgap MAE fell from 0.122 to 0.111 eV; frozen dev/test evaluation showed smaller gains, with transferability also evaluated on 3D perovskite solar cell efficiencies and Matbench structure-based splits.
infographic.watch_item: Deployment depends on whether training-only pseudo-OOD validation selects taxonomies that remain useful under the actual chemistry shift.
infographic.paper_title: MOTIF: LLM-Defined Material Taxonomies for OOD Property Prediction via Invariant Feature Selection

title: Neural network scaling and generalization for 3D strain fields in heterogeneous materials
authors: Lucas Fourel, Paul Devianne, Marine Debouvry, Tristan Destruhaut, Russell Gunn, Ashwini Gupta
abstract: Computational homogenization and coupled multiscale simulations of heterogeneous materials require repeated solution of mechanical fields on Representative Volume Elements, which becomes prohibitively expensive for high-resolution three-dimensional microstructures. Machine-learning surrogates can accelerate these computations, yet most existing approaches predict fields for fixed macroscopic loadings and provide limited guidance on how to scale network architectures for high-resolution 3D tensor-field prediction. This work presents a U-Net surrogate trained to predict the full 36-component strain localization tensor field in voxelized concrete mesostructures at resolutions up to $256^3$. Training localization tensors are generated with an FFT-based linear elastic solver, and an extensive hyperparameter optimization is performed to derive scaling rules and an accuracy-speed trade-off analysis. The results show that only network width and depth need to be scaled with problem complexity, while several conventional U-Net design choices, such as doubling channels after downsampling, are suboptimal for this problem. The final neural network achieves a Mean Absolute Error of 1.118% on both the validation and the held-out test sets, and an inference speedup of approximately 8.7x over the FFT-based solver on an Nvidia H100 GPU. Generalization experiments reveal transfer across aggregate volume fractions and highlight the importance of training on diverse morphologies. To safeguard reliability, a Maximum Mean Discrepancy metric computed on internal feature maps is proposed for detecting out-of-distribution microstructures without costly reference computations.

infographic.key_insight: A U-Net predicts full 36-component 3D strain localization tensor fields, with width and depth emerging as the key architecture scaling parameters.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The surrogate could accelerate repeated mechanical-field evaluations in concrete homogenization and coupled multiscale simulations.
method: Train on voxelized concrete mesostructures up to 256³ using localization tensors from an FFT-based linear elastic solver.
Optimize U-Net hyperparameters to identify architecture scaling rules and accuracy–speed trade-offs.
Use Maximum Mean Discrepancy on internal feature maps to flag out-of-distribution microstructures without reference solves.
infographic.evidence_signal: The final model achieved 1.118% Mean Absolute Error on both validation and held-out test sets and approximately 8.7× faster inference than the FFT solver on an Nvidia H100 GPU.
infographic.watch_item: Generalization depends on training morphology diversity; transfer across aggregate volume fractions does not establish reliability for arbitrary microstructures.
infographic.paper_title: Neural network scaling and generalization for 3D strain fields in heterogeneous materials

title: Adaptive catalyst discovery emerges from composable scientific intelligence
authors: Wentao Li, Qilong Cai, Qi Lei, Jinxing Chen, Ruixuan Chen, Jiangjie Qiu
abstract: Catalysis underpins chemical manufacturing, yet knowledge for catalyst design remains dispersed across experimental observations, computational data and catalysis subdisciplines. To overcome this challenge, we present Composable Catalytic Intelligence (CatAI), a physics-grounded modular AI framework that learns 1.8 million structure-property relations and organizes them into 30 physicochemical encoders. This reusable intermediate layer enables task-specific models to guide catalyst discovery for targeted reactions and objectives. Across benchmark tasks, CatAI achieves a 7.8% lower task-averaged prediction error than the next-best models. In experimental validation, CatAI identified a new confined-passable pocket catalyst applicable in industrial homogeneous polymer synthesis with 9 times the activity of the commercial benchmark. In parallel, it guided autonomous closed-loop optimization of a highly active Cu-based geminal-atom photocatalyst for C-O coupling reactions surpassing the traditional Ni-based systems. This approach connects property-level data to catalytic objectives, supporting physicochemical knowledge reuse across mechanistically distinct systems through computational screening and iterative model-experiment feedback.

infographic.key_insight: CatAI reuses modular physicochemical knowledge to guide catalyst discovery across mechanistically distinct reactions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework connects property data to catalytic objectives, supporting computational screening and iterative experimental optimization.
method: Learn from 1.8 million structure–property relations using 30 physicochemical encoders.
Compose reusable encoders into task-specific catalyst prediction models.
Guide candidate screening and autonomous model–experiment feedback loops.
infographic.evidence_signal: CatAI reports 7.8% lower task-averaged prediction error than next-best models, a polymer-synthesis catalyst with 9× commercial-benchmark activity, and a Cu-based photocatalyst outperforming traditional Ni-based systems.
infographic.watch_item: Transferability beyond the evaluated reactions and practical scale-up remain unestablished in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Adaptive catalyst discovery emerges from composable scientific intelligence

title: Out-of-the-Box Tabular Foundation Models for Bayesian Optimization in Materials Discovery
authors: Klemens Flöge, Simon Bing, Leo Grinsztajn, Eliott Kalfon, Lennart Purucker, Noah Hollmann
abstract: Bayesian optimization is widely used in active learning loops for materials science. Gaussian processes serve as the de-facto surrogate model family, but require task-dependent kernel choices and can lack the modeling capacity for complex relationships. Tabular foundation models (TFMs) have recently emerged as the state-of-the-art for predictive tasks on structured data, without requiring bespoke kernels or hyperparameter tuning. We evaluate two TFMs, TabPFN and TabICL, as out-of-the-box surrogate models on two standard materials science benchmarks, comparing against a large field of baselines encompassing Gaussian processes, random forests, and CatBoost. Our findings indicate that TFMs are highly competitive surrogate models across the two benchmarks, without task-specific training for active learning or GP kernel selection. Our results motivate developing TFMs further as surrogates for active learning in materials discovery.

infographic.key_insight: Out-of-the-box tabular foundation models are highly competitive Bayesian optimization surrogates for materials discovery, without task-specific training or Gaussian process kernel selection.
infographic.engineering_relevance: TabPFN and TabICL could reduce surrogate-model configuration effort in materials active learning workflows.
method: Use TabPFN and TabICL as out-of-the-box surrogate models.
Evaluate on two standard materials science benchmarks.
Compare against Gaussian processes, random forests, and CatBoost.

infographic.watch_item: Performance beyond the two evaluated benchmarks remains unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: Out-of-the-Box Tabular Foundation Models for Bayesian Optimization in Materials Discovery

title: Universal Multichannel Coherence-Mediated Thermal Transport in Carbon Allotropes: Experimental Evidence and Scaling Laws
authors: A. Jeżowski, A. I. Krivchikov, O. A. Korolyuk, V. V. Sagan, Y. V. Horbatenko, S. V. Cherednychenko
abstract: Understanding thermal transport in structurally disordered carbon materials remains a fundamental challenge because conventional models based on a single coherence contribution cannot accurately describe heat conduction over a broad temperature range. In this work, the thermal conductivity of graphene oxide (GO), thermally reduced graphene oxide (trGO), GO-hydrated fullerene composites (GO-HyFn), expanded graphite (EG), and EG-multiwalled carbon nanotube (MWCNT) composites was measured between 4.5 and 300 K. Despite substantial differences in density, porosity, graphitic ordering, and microstructure, all materials exhibit glass-like temperature dependence of thermal conductivity. The experimental results demonstrate that the conventional two-channel model, comprising a Peierls contribution and a single thermally activated coherence term, systematically fails to reproduce the observed temperature dependence. To resolve this discrepancy, we propose a generalized multichannel phenomenological model in which the coherence contribution consists of up to three Arrhenius-type channels with distinct activation energies. Depending on the structural state, two or three coherence channels are required to accurately describe the thermal conductivity. A key finding is the reproducible hierarchy of activation energies across diverse carbon allotropes, following approximately (E2 ~ 4E1 and E3 ~ (12-25)E1). While the channel amplitudes increase with material density, the activation energies remain nearly invariant, indicating universal vibrational energy scales. The proposed framework also consistently describes published data for other disordered carbon materials. These results provide experimental evidence for multichannel coherence-mediated heat transport and establish a unified phenomenological bridge between structural hierarchy with thermal transport in disordered carbon solids.

infographic.key_insight: Disordered carbon materials share glass-like thermal transport that is better described by two or three activated coherence channels with approximately recurring energy ratios.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework could improve temperature-dependent thermal conductivity models for porous and disordered carbon components across varied densities and microstructures.
method: Measure thermal conductivity from 4.5 to 300 K in GO, reduced GO, GO–hydrated fullerene, expanded graphite, and graphite–MWCNT composites.
Model transport using a Peierls contribution plus up to three Arrhenius-type coherence channels.
Compare activation energies and channel amplitudes across materials and with published disordered-carbon data.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports failure of the single-coherence-channel model, recurring ratios E2 ≈ 4E1 and E3 ≈ 12–25E1, and amplitudes that increase with density while activation energies remain nearly invariant.
infographic.watch_item: The model is phenomenological; the abstract provides no quantitative fit uncertainties or direct microscopic validation of the proposed coherence channels.
infographic.paper_title: Universal Multichannel Coherence-Mediated Thermal Transport in Carbon Allotropes: Experimental Evidence and Scaling Laws

title: Design of Self-Folding Origami Architectures for Biomedical Implants: A Finite Element Simulation Framework
authors: Suhas Chandrashekar, Thomas Stieglitz, Prasanth Velvaluri
abstract: Minimally invasive brain implants require compact deployment geometries and controlled shape transformation for delivery through confined vessels. Origami-inspired structures enable large shape changes from compact to tailored deployed configurations, but implementation at microscale dimensions remains challenging, as conventional designs rely on predefined mountain and valley folds that become increasingly difficult to fabricate and assemble as unit-cell size is reduced to meet clinical requirements. To address this, we propose a self-folding methodology based on thermally induced stresses in thin-film bimetallic composites. Pairing the shape memory alloy Nitinol (NiTi) with molybdenum or stainless steel (SS316L) exploits their differing thermal expansion coefficients to generate localized hinge bending, enabling deterministic, autonomous folding into prescribed mountain and valley configurations. Using finite element simulations, we systematically optimize hinge length, layer thickness, width, and shape, identifying a hinge geometry achieving a ~50% reduction in unit-cell dimensions relative to previously reported designs. Integration into a complete waterbomb origami unit cell confirms that the strip-level folding mechanism scales to produce coordinated, self-folding deformation across the tessellated structure. These results demonstrate the feasibility of stress-induced, self-folding thin-film origami architectures built from clinically established biomaterials, providing a scalable design framework for next-generation, active neurovascular implants with integrated sensing and monitoring functionality.

infographic.key_insight: Finite element simulations suggest thermally stressed NiTi-based bilayer hinges can drive autonomous mountain and valley folding in microscale origami implant architectures.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Compact, self-folding structures could support minimally invasive neurovascular implant delivery and controlled deployment.
method: Pair NiTi with molybdenum or SS316L to generate hinge bending through thermal expansion mismatch.
Optimize hinge length, layer thickness, width, and shape using finite element simulations.
Integrate optimized hinges into a waterbomb origami unit cell to evaluate coordinated folding.
infographic.evidence_signal: Simulations identified a hinge geometry enabling approximately 50% smaller unit-cell dimensions than previously reported designs and demonstrated coordinated folding in a complete waterbomb unit cell.
infographic.watch_item: Experimental validation is still needed to establish fabrication reliability and safe thermal actuation under physiological conditions.
infographic.paper_title: Design of Self-Folding Origami Architectures for Biomedical Implants: A Finite Element Simulation Framework

title: Elastic Landau states as martensite nuclei in austenite
authors: Mohd Tahseen, Vivekanand Dabade
abstract: In this article, we investigate the geometric closure of austenite--martensite interfaces. Classical compatibility conditions permit stress-free interfaces between the two phases: the condition $λ_2 = 1$ admits planar interfaces, whereas the cofactor conditions additionally admit curved interfaces. However, neither, guarantees the geometric closure of these interfaces. We identify two-parameter families of martensitic deformations that overcome this limitation and enable the formation of closed, stress-free martensite nuclei embedded in an austenite matrix. A main result is the interpretation of the classical deformation modes of simple shear and pure shear as martensitic phase transformations. These correspond to cubic to monoclinic-II and cubic to orthorhombic transformations, respectively. The former naturally satisfies the \emph{extreme compatibility conditions}, which are stronger than the cofactor conditions, and gives rise to \emph{elastic Landau states}, a self-accommodating martensitic nuclei embedded in austenite. We show that these states can be assembled to form arbitrarily shaped, stress-free martensitic islands surrounded by austenite. Such states can arise even in conventional shape memory alloys that do not satisfy supercompatibility, provided hierarchical twinning produces an average deformation that is a simple shear. The theory provides a geometric mechanism for self-accommodation. Its predicted deformation gradients agree with those reconstructed from experimentally observed microstructures. This agreement suggests that these microstructures originate from simple shear.

infographic.key_insight: Simple-shear martensitic transformations enable elastic Landau states that assemble into closed, stress-free martensite islands within austenite.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The theory offers geometric guidance for designing self-accommodating transformation microstructures in shape-memory alloys, including through hierarchical twinning.
method: Identify two-parameter deformation families that permit closed, stress-free austenite–martensite interfaces.
Interpret simple shear and pure shear as cubic-to-monoclinic-II and cubic-to-orthorhombic transformations, respectively.
Assemble elastic Landau states into arbitrarily shaped martensitic islands.
infographic.evidence_signal: Predicted deformation gradients agree with gradients reconstructed from experimentally observed microstructures, although the abstract reports no quantitative agreement metrics.
infographic.watch_item: Geometric compatibility alone does not establish whether the proposed nuclei form under realistic energetic and kinetic constraints.
infographic.paper_title: Elastic Landau states as martensite nuclei in austenite

title: How anion composition governs structural frameworks and Li-ion transport in oxychloride solid-state electrolytes
authors: Jiho Lee, Seungwoo Hwang, Seungwu Han, Jisu Jung, Youngho Kang, Sungwoo Kang
abstract: Mixed-anion lithium oxychlorides exhibit high Li conductivity, but the relationship between oxygen content, structural framework, and Li-ion transport remains unclear. Here, crystal structure prediction and molecular dynamics simulations with machine-learning interatomic potentials are used to examine $\mathrm{Li}_yM\mathrm{O}_x\mathrm{Cl}_{6-2x}$ ($M$ = Nb and Ta [Group 5] and $M$ = Ti, Zr, and Hf [Group 4]). Increasing oxygen content changes isolated chloride-rich polyhedra into one-dimensional chains and subsequently more highly connected two- and three-dimensional frameworks. In the Group 5 series, fast Li diffusion occurs over $x \approx 0.67$--1.5, where the Li sites form a three-dimensional percolating network. Potential of mean force maps and nudged elastic band calculations reveal that fast Li-ion transport requires a low-dimensional framework supporting long-range migration through undercoordinated Li sites with low barriers, together with similar energies across Li sites. Finally, we perform fine-grid compositional search, which identifies $\mathrm{LiNbO}_{0.67}\mathrm{Cl}_{4.67}$, $\mathrm{LiTaO}_{0.75}\mathrm{Cl}_{4.5}$, $\mathrm{LiNbO}_{1.5}\mathrm{Cl}_3$, and $\mathrm{LiTaO}_{1.5}\mathrm{Cl}_3$ as stable candidates with predicted room-temperature self-diffusivities of up to $\sim 10^{-6}\,\mathrm{cm}^2/\mathrm{s}$. These findings establish how oxygen content controls framework and Li-ion transport, guiding the design of lithium oxyhalide electrolytes.

infographic.key_insight: Oxygen content controls oxychloride framework connectivity, with fast Li-ion transport favored by low-dimensional frameworks that support three-dimensional migration through low-barrier, similar-energy Li sites.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Tuning the oxygen-to-chlorine ratio offers a design route to solid electrolytes with predicted room-temperature Li self-diffusivities up to approximately 10⁻⁶ cm²/s.
method: Crystal structure prediction and molecular dynamics using machine-learning interatomic potentials.
Potential-of-mean-force mapping and nudged elastic band calculations of Li migration.
Fine-grid compositional search across Nb-, Ta-, Ti-, Zr-, and Hf-based oxychlorides.
infographic.evidence_signal: Simulations find fast Li diffusion in Nb/Ta compositions at oxygen content x ≈ 0.67–1.5 and identify four stable candidates: LiNbO₀.₆₇Cl₄.₆₇, LiTaO₀.₇₅Cl₄.₅, LiNbO₁.₅Cl₃, and LiTaO₁.₅Cl₃.
infographic.watch_item: The stability and transport results are computational predictions; experimental synthesis and ionic-conductivity measurements are needed to validate practical electrolyte performance.
infographic.paper_title: How anion composition governs structural frameworks and Li-ion transport in oxychloride solid-state electrolytes

title: Effect of Correlation on the Pressure-Induced Insulator to Metal Transition in Complex Spin-Orbit Coupled Double Perovskite La$_2$CoIr$_{1-x}$Ti$_x$O$_6$
authors: Vineeta Yadav, Sromona Nandi, Rudra Sekhar Manna
abstract: We study the effect of electron correlation ($U$) and hydrostatic pressure on the electronic properties of double perovskites La$_2$CoIr$_{1-x}$Ti$_x$O$_6$ for $x$ = 0, 0.5, and 1, using first-principles electronic structure calculations within density functional theory (DFT). At ambient pressure, we systematically vary the electron correlation, i.e., on-site Coulomb interaction to study its effect on band gap and structural parameters. Increasing the value of $U$ enhances the band gap of all three compositions while producing only a slight variation in structural parameters. The effect of hydrostatic pressure is also studied for the same compositions. The estimated band gap values at ambient pressure closes at approximately 39, 42, and 53 GPa for $x$ = 0 (for $U_\mathrm{Co}$ = 5 eV and $U_\mathrm{Ir}$ = 2 eV), 0.5 (for $U_\mathrm{Co}$ = 5 eV and $U_\mathrm{Ir}$ = 2 eV), and 1 (for $U_\mathrm{Co}$ = 4 eV), respectively, indicating pressure-induced insulator-to-metal transitions. These results show that electron correlation stabilises the insulating state, whereas hydrostatic pressure favours the metallic state by closing the band gap. These findings highlight the tunability of correlated oxides through electron correlations and pressure, offering insights for materials design.

infographic.key_insight: In La₂CoIr₁₋ₓTiₓO₆, stronger electron correlation widens the insulating band gap, while hydrostatic pressure closes it and induces a metallic state.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Composition, electron correlation, and pressure offer complementary levers for tuning electronic behavior in correlated double perovskites.
method: First-principles DFT calculations for x = 0, 0.5, and 1.
Varied on-site Coulomb interaction U at ambient pressure to assess band gaps and structural parameters.
Applied hydrostatic pressure to predict band-gap closure.
infographic.evidence_signal: Predicted gap closure occurs near 39, 42, and 53 GPa for x = 0, 0.5, and 1, respectively, using UCo = 5 eV and UIr = 2 eV for the first two compositions and UCo = 4 eV for the third.
infographic.watch_item: Transition pressures depend on the chosen correlation parameters, and the abstract reports no experimental validation.
infographic.paper_title: Effect of Correlation on the Pressure-Induced Insulator to Metal Transition in Complex Spin-Orbit Coupled Double Perovskite La$_2$CoIr$_{1-x}$Ti$_x$O$_6$

title: Quantum Embedding from Molecular to Crystalline Environments at the Cost of a Gas-Phase Calculation
authors: Manas Sharma, Marek Sierka
abstract: We present a direct-space formulation and implementation of quantum density functional theory (DFT) embedding for molecular active subsystems embedded in frozen environments (hosts) of arbitrary dimensionality, from finite molecular hosts to extended systems. The host is computed once without the embedded molecule (the guest) and is represented only by its electron density fitted in an atom-centered auxiliary Gaussian basis together with its nuclear charges with the periodic electrostatics separated into an explicit near-field and a continuous fast-multipole far-field operator. The method allows the removal of host atoms from this representation to create vacancies or other voids without requiring a supercell creation. Analytic nuclear gradients are also implemented, enabling structural relaxation of the active subsystem. We demonstrate the versatility of the approach through applications to adsorbates on periodic surfaces and molecules embedded in bulk solvent environments. For CO on MgO(001), we show that DFT-in-DFT converges rapidly and reproduces the periodic interaction energy within 0.44 kJ/mol while reducing the cost by a factor of 27. Real-time time-dependent embedded DFT (RT-TDDFET) of methylenecyclopropene in periodic water is showcased to produce a ~0.6 eV solvatochromic blue shift, while strong-field propagation of CO2 on hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) yields substrate-induced effects at the cost of a gas-phase propagation. Coupling the embedding scheme to excited-state correlated wave function theory methods such as CC2 yields a solvent shift within 0.01 eV of supermolecular CC2 references, while reducing the computational cost by over 500 times.

infographic.key_insight: Quantum embedding captures molecular behavior in finite or crystalline environments while keeping active-subsystem calculations near gas-phase cost.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach enables efficient simulations of adsorption, solvent effects, and light-driven molecular dynamics without repeatedly computing the full surrounding material.
method: Compute the frozen host once and represent it using Gaussian-fitted electron density and nuclear charges.
Separate periodic electrostatics into explicit near-field and fast-multipole far-field contributions.
Use analytic gradients to relax the active subsystem and remove host atoms to create voids without supercells.
infographic.evidence_signal: Reported benchmarks include CO/MgO interaction energies within 0.44 kJ/mol of periodic DFT at 27× lower cost and a solvent shift within 0.01 eV of supermolecular CC2 at over 500× lower cost.
infographic.watch_item: The frozen-host approximation warrants validation when guest-induced polarization or structural changes in the environment are important.
infographic.paper_title: Quantum Embedding from Molecular to Crystalline Environments at the Cost of a Gas-Phase Calculation

title: Defects and Structural Evolution in CrSBr: Machine-Learning Potentials for Atomistic Simulations
authors: Arsalan Hashemi, Daniil Kruklinskii, Xiaoya Chang, Tapio Ala-Nissila, Mikko Karttunen, Arkady V. Krasheninnikov
abstract: The layered van der Waals semiconductor CrSBr combines intrinsic magnetic order with semiconducting and optical properties, making it a promising material for multifunctional electronic and photonic applications. Understanding how defects and structural transformations affect its properties under experimentally relevant conditions, however, remains challenging for first-principles simulations due to the relevant length and time scales. Here, we develop and benchmark machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) for the Cr-S-Br system, enabling large-scale atomistic simulations of CrSBr with accuracy approaching that of density functional theory (DFT). The charge-aware variant qNEP achieves near-DFT accuracy in predicting lattice constants, formation enthalpies, vacancy energetics, and the anisotropic pressure response of o-CrSBr. Nudged elastic band calculations reveal that pre-existing S vacancies lower the Cr Frenkel-pair migration barrier by up to 1.1 eV, providing an atomistic mechanism for beam-induced Cr redistribution and structural transformations. Displacement threshold calculations further show that Br is the most susceptible species to electron-beam-induced displacement, identifying the relative ease of removing different atomic species. Together, these results establish a validated computational framework for investigating atomic-scale disorder and structural transformations in CrSBr, providing a basis for defect engineering in materials for future magneto-optoelectronic applications.

infographic.key_insight: Charge-aware machine-learning potentials enable near-DFT modeling of CrSBr and reveal that sulfur vacancies can lower chromium Frenkel-pair migration barriers by up to 1.1 eV.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework supports large-scale studies of defect engineering and beam-induced structural changes in CrSBr for future magneto-optoelectronic applications.
method: Develop and benchmark Cr–S–Br machine-learning interatomic potentials, including charge-aware qNEP.
Use nudged elastic band calculations to assess vacancy-assisted chromium migration.
Calculate displacement thresholds to compare species susceptibility to electron-beam damage.
infographic.evidence_signal: qNEP achieves near-DFT accuracy for lattice constants, formation enthalpies, vacancy energetics, and anisotropic pressure response; displacement calculations identify Br as the most susceptible species.
infographic.watch_item: Accuracy beyond the benchmarked structures and defect environments remains to be established.
infographic.paper_title: Defects and Structural Evolution in CrSBr: Machine-Learning Potentials for Atomistic Simulations

title: Point defects and primary radiation damage in Co-free Fe-Ni-Cr-Mn high-entropy alloys from molecular dynamics
authors: Ayobami Daramola, Giovanni Bonny, Gilles Adjanor, Christophe Domain, Ghiath Monnet, Anna Fraczkiewicz
abstract: Co-free Fe-Ni-Cr-Mn high-entropy alloys (HEAs) are candidates for nuclear structural applications. We used molecular dynamics with the EAM-21 potential, stiffened at short range, to study five HEAs that have been irradiated experimentally: Fe37Ni34Cr16Mn13 (ES1), Fe35Ni35Cr15Mn15 (P35), Fe46Ni22Cr15Mn17 (Y3), Fe27Ni28Cr18Mn27 (Kumar) and Fe30Ni30Cr10Mn30 (C30). They were compared with pure Ni, Fe60Ni40, the Fe70Ni10Cr20 model alloy of 316L, and Fe50Ni34Cr16, which is ES1 with Mn replaced by Fe. We calculated stacking fault energies, threshold displacement energies, point-defect formation and migration energies, and 1015 displacement cascades from 5 to 40 keV at 300 and 823 K. The stacking fault energy follows the Ni content: 19-44 mJ/m^2 in the alloys and 113 mJ/m^2 in Ni. Compared with the Mn-free alloys, the HEAs have lower threshold displacement energies (48-56 against 64-74 eV) and lower dumbbell formation energies, and Mn is the element most transported by interstitials. All the concentrated alloys leave about the same number of Frenkel pairs, 56-72 at 40 keV, half the number in Ni. At 40 keV, 54-58% of the interstitials are in clusters in the HEAs, against 67-71% in Fe60Ni40, Fe70Ni10Cr20 and Fe50Ni34Cr16 and 82% in Ni. At the same cluster size, clusters of 4-12 interstitials are faulted about half as often in the HEAs, and this does not follow the stacking fault energy. The surviving interstitials are enriched in Mn in the HEAs and in Ni in the Mn-free alloys, and depleted in Cr. The results support direct loop formation in cascades in Fe60Ni40 and Fe70Ni10Cr20 and less of it in ES1.

infographic.key_insight: Co-free Fe-Ni-Cr-Mn alloys retain roughly half as many cascade-induced Frenkel pairs as pure Ni and show less interstitial clustering than Mn-free comparison alloys.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These defect-production trends support evaluating Co-free alloys for nuclear structural applications, but do not establish long-term irradiation performance.
method: Molecular dynamics with a short-range-stiffened EAM-21 potential.
Compared five Co-free HEAs with Ni and three Mn-free alloys.
Calculated defect energetics and simulated 1,015 cascades at 5–40 keV and 300/823 K.
infographic.evidence_signal: At 40 keV, concentrated alloys retained 56–72 Frenkel pairs, about half the Ni count; interstitial clustering was 54–58% in HEAs versus 67–71% in Mn-free alloys and 82% in Ni.
infographic.watch_item: Results depend on the interatomic potential and describe primary cascade damage, not long-term defect evolution under sustained irradiation.
infographic.paper_title: Point defects and primary radiation damage in Co-free Fe-Ni-Cr-Mn high-entropy alloys from molecular dynamics

title: High Pressure Material Phase Identification with Gaussian Kernel Neural Networks
authors: Cameron Ryan, Yasantha Pasindu Hetti Kankanamalage, Shuai Zhang
abstract: Phase identification is a computational task involving the classification of material structure using the positions of atoms. Using data from Molecular Dynamics (MD) simulations, our task is to identify the material phase of a set of atoms, based on how the simulations predict their positioning relative to each other. By leveraging existing research on mechanistic neural network theory, particularly Neural Tangent Kernels (NTK), we develop a new and efficient method for classifying simulated material samples. Our method involves defining a set of "atom detectors" that are given positions around the origin in cartesian coordinates. The sum of Gaussians centered at each atom is calculated at each atom detector, and is used as the input to a neural network. We present theoretical and experimental evidence to show that this method is highly effective and efficient at the task. Our method obtains better or similar accuracy scores to commonly used methods while having a major computational speedup.

infographic.key_insight: Gaussian atom-density features enable a neural network to identify simulated material phases with comparable or better accuracy and substantially faster computation than commonly used methods.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Faster phase identification could accelerate structural analysis of high-pressure molecular dynamics simulations.
method: Place virtual atom detectors at Cartesian positions around the origin.
At each detector, sum Gaussian contributions centered on the atoms.
Feed detector values into a neural network informed by Neural Tangent Kernel theory.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical and experimental support using molecular dynamics data, but provides no numerical accuracy or speedup results.
infographic.watch_item: Generalization across materials and simulation conditions is not established by the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: High Pressure Material Phase Identification with Gaussian Kernel Neural Networks

title: Fine-Tuning an Order-Flow Foundation Model for Sub-Second Forecasting
authors: Fedor Shabashev
abstract: Generative models have become the standard approach in language and vision. These models are typically pretrained first and then fine-tuned. Recent work demonstrates how to pretrain an autoregressive generative model on Level-3 order-flow data. However, to our knowledge, no one has fine-tuned such a model yet for downstream tasks. Here we first pretrain a 300M-parameter generative model on Level-3 order-flow data collected from two crypto exchanges, Bitstamp and Bitfinex. Then we fine-tune the pretrained model to predict the microprice return and its realized volatility. We show that our fine-tuned model outperforms classical baselines, such as gradient boosting on handcrafted features, in predicting microprice returns over sub-second horizons. Furthermore, the predictive ability of the model transfers zero-shot to assets it was never fine-tuned on. Due to the short-term nature of these forecasts, the predicted microprice moves are smaller than the bid-ask spread plus fees, so the natural applications are in execution and market making. These results indicate that a pretrained generative model can be turned into a competitive short-horizon price forecaster via fine-tuning.

infographic.key_insight: Fine-tuning a pretrained order-flow model enables competitive sub-second price forecasting; this paper concerns financial markets, not materials science.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The forecasts could support trade execution and market making rather than standalone directional trading.
method: Pretrain a 300M-parameter autoregressive model on Level-3 order-flow data from Bitstamp and Bitfinex.
Fine-tune it to predict microprice returns and realized volatility.
Evaluate return forecasts against classical baselines and test zero-shot transfer to unseen assets.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports better sub-second microprice-return prediction than classical baselines, including gradient boosting on handcrafted features, and zero-shot transfer to assets excluded from fine-tuning.
infographic.watch_item: Predicted price moves are smaller than the bid-ask spread plus fees, limiting direct trading profitability.
infographic.paper_title: Fine-Tuning an Order-Flow Foundation Model for Sub-Second Forecasting

title: Learning Electronic Band Structures Across the s, p, d Blocks with an Empirical Pseudopotential Network
authors: Qiang Zhu
abstract: Electronic band structures govern how crystals conduct electrons and absorb light. Density-functional theory (DFT) computes them through costly self-consistent iterations, while existing machine-learning models either predict isolated scalar properties or output Hamiltonians that still require DFT solvers. Here we present EpNet, a learned empirical pseudopotential for crystals spanning 63 elements across the \textit{s}, \textit{p} and \textit{d} blocks. An equivariant neural network builds its Hamiltonian from physics-motivated local potentials and nonlocal projectors. Trained solely on band energies, EpNet predicts complete band structures directly from atomic coordinates. On unseen chemical systems, its median errors are \winAll\ eV for band energies and \gapAll\ eV for band gaps. On 600,000 structures from an independent database, its band-gap errors are overall less than half those of existing models, at about 1\% of DFT cost. EpNet thus enables fast screening of electronic properties for materials discovery and electronic-structure simulations of large systems.

infographic.key_insight: EpNet learns empirical pseudopotentials to predict complete crystal band structures directly from atomic coordinates across 63 s-, p-, and d-block elements.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Electronic-property screening at about 1% of DFT cost could accelerate materials discovery and enable electronic-structure simulations of larger systems.
method: Use an equivariant neural network to construct a Hamiltonian from local potentials and nonlocal projectors.
Train solely on band energies rather than Hamiltonian labels.
Predict band structures without DFT self-consistent iterations.
infographic.evidence_signal: On 600,000 structures from an independent database, the abstract reports overall band-gap errors less than half those of existing models.
infographic.watch_item: Exact median band-energy and band-gap errors are unresolved placeholders in the abstract, limiting assessment of absolute accuracy.
infographic.paper_title: Learning Electronic Band Structures Across the s, p, d Blocks with an Empirical Pseudopotential Network

title: Towards Multiscale Molecular Representation Learning through Geometry-Based Fragmentation for Polymer Property Prediction
authors: Makoto Takamoto, Chaitanya Sampara, Viktor Zaverkin, Daniel Oñoro-Rubio, Mathias Niepert
abstract: It is well established that molecular substructures can contribute unequally to chemical and physical properties, with specific motifs or side chains often playing dominant roles. Fragment-based representations have therefore emerged as an effective strategy for incorporating chemically meaningful inductive biases, as exemplified by molecular fingerprints and fragment-based attention mechanisms. However, many existing fragmentation-based machine learning methods rely on predefined chemical rules, which may yield suboptimal fragmentation for previously unseen or chemically unfamiliar structures and often overlook the importance of multiscale molecular representations. To address these limitations, we formulate molecular fragmentation as a radius-constrained optimization problem inspired by the k-center formulation, where the number of clusters is not fixed a priori but emerges from the specified radius, and propose a geometry-based fragmentation method that partitions arbitrary molecular or material structures using largely geometric information, without relying on predefined chemical fragmentation rules. The method provides flexible control over fragment size, enabling the construction of multiscale fragment representations for scale-adaptive modeling. Building on this framework, we develop a geometric fragment-based attention mechanism that integrates multiscale structural information and incorporate it into a multimodal machine learning model combining p-SMILES representations with three-dimensional (3D) conformational information. Experiments on a benchmark polymer dataset show that incorporating 3D conformational information improves prediction accuracy for several properties over models based exclusively on p-SMILES representations. Explainable artificial intelligence analyses further provide insights into the physical relevance of the learned representations.

infographic.key_insight: Geometry-based fragmentation enables multiscale polymer representations without predefined chemical fragmentation rules.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Combining polymer sequence notation with 3D structural information can improve property prediction for materials screening.
method: Formulate fragmentation as a radius-constrained optimization inspired by k-center, with fragment count determined by the radius.
Vary the radius to construct multiscale fragments using largely geometric information.
Integrate fragment-based attention into a multimodal model combining p-SMILES and 3D conformations.
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments on a benchmark polymer dataset show improved prediction accuracy for several properties when adding 3D conformational information; explainability analyses probe physical relevance.
infographic.watch_item: Practical performance may depend on conformer quality and fragmentation radius; the abstract does not quantify sensitivity to either.
infographic.paper_title: Towards Multiscale Molecular Representation Learning through Geometry-Based Fragmentation for Polymer Property Prediction

title: Ultrafast Hole Transport and Electron Localization in Superatomic Re$_{6}$Se$_{8}$Cl$_{2}$
authors: Jocelyn L. Mendes-Antaya, Ye-Jin Kim, Jonathan M. Michelsen, Jessica Yu, Shoushou He, Xavier Roy
abstract: Van der Waals superatomic crystals represent an intriguing class of materials, exhibiting unique ultrafast electronic and structural responses arising from their hierarchical crystal structure. These materials bridge the properties of semiconductors, molecular solids, and nanocrystal arrays, hosting a range of many-body interactions that can be controlled with atomically precise structures. To establish the structure-function correlation, it is necessary to understand element-specific electronic states arising from complex superatomic unit cells. Here, we use transient XUV spectroscopy to individually probe the dynamics of photoexcited electrons and holes in Re$_{6}$Se$_{8}$Cl$_{2}$ superatomic crystals. We simultaneously measure photodynamics at the Re O$_{2}$ and Se M$_{4,5}$ edges, enabling decomposition of excited-state dynamics into the contributions of electron, hole, band gap, and phonon dynamics occurring around Re and Se atoms. By correlating spectral features at the Re and Se edges, we infer the existence of flat conduction bands and identify hot hole transfer from Re to Se atoms. We observe phonon oscillations driven by hole-mediated displacive excitations. The measurements highlight that the photodynamics are dominated by charge transfer between metallic sites which drives phonon coupling in the nonequilibrium state. This work provides insights into the optoelectronic applications of superatomic crystals for future tuning of emergent material properties.

infographic.key_insight: Element-specific spectroscopy reveals ultrafast hole transfer from Re to Se and electron localization associated with inferred flat conduction bands in Re₆Se₈Cl₂ superatomic crystals.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Understanding site-specific charge transfer and phonon coupling could guide tuning of superatomic crystals for optoelectronic applications.
method: Probe photoexcited carriers with transient XUV spectroscopy.
Simultaneously measure the Re O₂ and Se M₄,₅ absorption edges.
Correlate spectral features to separate electron, hole, band-gap, and phonon dynamics.
infographic.evidence_signal: Correlated Re- and Se-edge measurements indicate hot-hole transfer and reveal phonon oscillations attributed to hole-mediated displacive excitation.
infographic.watch_item: Flat conduction bands are inferred from spectroscopy, and the abstract reports no device-level performance validation.
infographic.paper_title: Ultrafast Hole Transport and Electron Localization in Superatomic Re$_{6}$Se$_{8}$Cl$_{2}$
